message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and ensure safe, habitable living conditions. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge a security deposit up to **one month’s rent** for residential units.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear.
• Landlord must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep records of move‑in condition (photos, videos).
• Request a written receipt for the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a **safe and livable condition**: functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.
• Must comply with local building, health, and safety codes. | • Document any repairs needed.
• If landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (see below). | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If the landlord fails to repair a **material defect** within **30 days** of notice, you may:
 1. Pay the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent.
 2. Withhold rent until the issue is fixed.
 3. Terminate the lease if the defect is unrepairable. | • Provide written notice to the landlord.
• Keep receipts for any repairs you pay. | | **Notice Requirements** | • **Rent increase**: Landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** for increases less than 25% of current rent; **90 days** for increases ≥25%.
• **Termination of tenancy**: For month‑to‑month leases, 30 days’ notice is required.
• **Eviction**: Must follow the proper legal process (notice, court filing, judgment). | • Verify that any notice you receive meets the statutory time frame. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlord may enter only for **reasonable purposes** (repairs, inspections, showing to prospective tenants/buyers).
• Must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes (under the federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Act). | • Report any discriminatory actions to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for leases longer than one year.
• Certain terms are prohibited (e.g., requiring a tenant to waive their right to a jury trial). | • Review lease carefully before signing. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide a written statement of utility responsibilities.
• If utilities are included, they must be maintained in working order. | • Clarify who pays which utilities. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Tenants may sublet or assign the lease with the landlord’s written consent (unless the lease prohibits it). | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates any of the above, tenants can:
 1. File a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office.
 2. Seek a court order to compel compliance.
 3. Sue for damages or attorney’s fees. | • Keep all documentation (emails, texts, photos, receipts). | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help prove your case if disputes arise. 2. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Look for clauses that might limit your rights (e.g., “no subletting” or “no rent withholding”). 3. **Know the Statutory Time Frames** – For example, the 30‑day notice for repairs or rent increases. 4. **Communicate in Writing** – Email or text is preferable to phone calls because it creates a record. 5. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you’re unsure about a clause or suspect a violation, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local tenant‑advocacy organization. ### Resources - **Texas Property Code, Chapter 24** – The primary statute governing residential landlord‑tenant relations. - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** – Offers guidance and can investigate complaints. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – Handles discrimination complaints. - **Local Tenant‑Advocacy Groups** – Many cities have nonprofits that provide free or low‑cost legal assistance. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney familiar with Texas landlord‑tenant law.
